paragraphs:
Now that war and the problems of war are things of the past, I
think I may safely venture to reveal to the world the part which
my friend Poirot played in a moment of national crisis. The secret
has been well guarded. Not a whisper of it reached the Press. But,
now that the need for secrecy has gone by, I feel it is only just
that England should know the debt it owes to my quaint little
friend, whose marvellous brain so ably averted a great catastrophe.

One evening after dinner—I will not particularize the date; it
suffices to say that it was at the time when “Peace by negotiation”
was the parrot-cry of England’s enemies—my friend and I were
sitting in his rooms. After being invalided out of the Army I had
been given a recruiting job, and it had become my custom to drop
in on Poirot in the evenings after dinner and talk with him of any
cases of interest that he might have on hand.

I was attempting to discuss with him the sensational news of that
day—no less than an attempted assassination of Mr. David MacAdam,
England’s Prime Minister. The account in the papers had evidently
been carefully censored. No details were given, save that the Prime
Minister had had a marvellous escape, the bullet just grazing his
cheek.

I considered that our police must have been shamefully careless
for such an outrage to be possible. I could well understand that
the German agents in England would be willing to risk much for such
an achievement. “Fighting Mac,” as his own party had nicknamed him,
had strenuously and unequivocally combated the Pacifist influence
which was becoming so prevalent.

He was more than England’s Prime Minister—he _was_ England; and
to have removed him from his sphere of influence would have been
a crushing and paralysing blow to Britain.

Poirot was busy mopping a grey suit with a minute sponge. Never
was there a dandy such as Hercule Poirot. Neatness and order were
his passion. Now, with the odour of benzine filling the air, he
was quite unable to give me his full attention.

“In a little minute I am with you, my friend. I have all but
finished. The spot of grease—he is not good—I remove him—so!” He
waved his sponge.

I smiled as I lit another cigarette.

“Anything interesting on?” I inquired, after a minute or two.

“I assist a—how do you call it?—‘charlady’ to find her husband. A
difficult affair, needing the tact. For I have a little idea that
when he is found he will not be pleased. What would you? For my
part, I sympathize with him. He was a man of discrimination to lose
himself.”

I laughed.

“At last! The spot of grease, he is gone! I am at your disposal.”

“I was asking you what you thought of this attempt to assassinate
MacAdam?”

“_Enfantillage!_” replied Poirot promptly. “One can hardly take it
seriously. To fire with the rifle—never does it succeed. It is a
device of the past.”

“It was very near succeeding this time,” I reminded him.

Poirot shook his head impatiently. He was about to reply when the
landlady thrust her head round the door and informed him that there
were two gentlemen below who wanted to see him.

“They won’t give their names, sir, but they says as it’s very
important.”

“Let them mount,” said Poirot, carefully folding his grey trousers.

In a few minutes the two visitors were ushered in, and my heart
gave a leap as in the foremost I recognized no less a personage
than Lord Estair, Leader of the House of Commons; whilst his
companion, Mr. Bernard Dodge, was also a member of the War Cabinet,
and, as I knew, a close personal friend of the Prime Minister.

“Monsieur Poirot?” said Lord Estair interrogatively. My friend
bowed. The great man looked at me and hesitated. “My business is
private.”

“You may speak freely before Captain Hastings,” said my friend,
nodding to me to remain. “He has not all the gifts, no! But I
answer for his discretion.”

Lord Estair still hesitated, but Mr. Dodge broke in abruptly:

“Oh, come on—don’t let’s beat about the bush! As far as I can see,
the whole of England will know the hole we’re in soon enough.
Time’s everything.”

“Pray be seated, messieurs,” said Poirot politely. “Will you take
the big chair, _milord_?”

Lord Estair started slightly. “You know me?”

Poirot smiled. “Certainly. I read the little papers with the
pictures. How should I not know you?”

“Monsieur Poirot, I have come to consult you upon a matter of the
most vital urgency. I must ask for absolute secrecy.”

“You have the word of Hercule Poirot—I can say no more!” said my
friend grandiloquently.

“It concerns the Prime Minister. We are in grave trouble.”

“We’re up a tree!” interposed Mr. Dodge.

“The injury is serious, then?” I asked.

“What injury?”

“The bullet wound.”

“Oh, that!” cried Mr. Dodge contemptuously. “That’s old history.”

“As my colleague says,” continued Lord Estair, “that affair is over
and done with. Luckily, it failed. I wished I could say as much
for the second attempt.”

“There has been a second attempt, then?”

“Yes, though not of the same nature. Monsieur Poirot, the Prime
Minister has disappeared.”

“What?”

“He has been kidnapped!”

“Impossible!” I cried, stupefied.

Poirot threw a withering glance at me, which I knew enjoined me to
keep my mouth shut.

“Unfortunately, impossible as it seems, it is only too true,”
continued his lordship.

Poirot looked at Mr. Dodge. “You said just now, monsieur, that time
was everything. What did you mean by that?”

The two men exchanged glances, and then Lord Estair said:

“You have heard, Monsieur Poirot, of the approaching Allied
Conference?”

My friend nodded.

“For obvious reasons, no details have been given of when and where
it is to take place. But, although it has been kept out of the
newspapers, the date is, of course, widely known in diplomatic
circles. The Conference is to be held to-morrow—Thursday—evening
at Versailles. Now you perceive the terrible gravity of the
situation. I will not conceal from you that the Prime Minister’s
presence at the Conference is a vital necessity. The Pacifist
propaganda, started and maintained by the German agents in our
midst, has been very active. It is the universal opinion that the
turning point of the Conference will be the strong personality of
the Prime Minister. His absence may have the most serious
results—possibly a premature and disastrous peace. And we have no
one who can be sent in his place. He alone can represent England.”

Poirot’s face had grown very grave. “Then you regard the kidnapping
of the Prime Minister as a direct attempt to prevent his being
present at the Conference?”

“Most certainly I do. He was actually on his way to France at the
time.”

“And the Conference is to be held?”

“At nine o’clock to-morrow night.”

Poirot drew an enormous watch from his pocket.

“It is now a quarter to nine.”

“Twenty-four hours,” said Mr. Dodge thoughtfully.

“And a quarter,” amended Poirot. “Do not forget the quarter,
monsieur—it may come in useful. Now for the details—the abduction,
did it take place in England or in France?”

“In France. Mr. MacAdam crossed to France this morning. He was to
stay to-night as the guest of the Commander-in-Chief, proceeding
to-morrow to Paris. He was conveyed across the Channel by destroyer.
At Boulogne he was met by a car from General Headquarters and one
of the Commander-in-Chief’s A.D.C.s.”

“_Eh bien_?”

“Well, they started from Boulogne—but they never arrived.”

“What?”

“Monsieur Poirot, it was a bogus car and a bogus A.D.C. The real
car was found in a side road, with the chauffeur and the A.D.C.
neatly gagged and bound.”

“And the bogus car?”

“Is still at large.”

Poirot made a gesture of impatience. “Incredible! Surely it cannot
escape attention for long?”

“So we thought. It seemed merely a question of searching thoroughly.
That part of France is under Military Law. We were convinced that
the car could not go long unnoticed. The French police and our own
Scotland Yard men, and the military are straining every nerve. It
is, as you say, incredible—but nothing has been discovered!”

At that moment a tap came at the door, and a young officer entered
with a heavily sealed envelope which he handed to Lord Estair.

“Just through from France, sir. I brought it on here, as you
directed.”

The Minister tore it open eagerly, and uttered an exclamation. The
officer withdrew.

“Here is news at last! This telegram has just been decoded. They
have found the second car, also the secretary, Daniels, chloroformed,
gagged, and bound, in an abandoned farm near C——. He remembers
nothing, except something being pressed against his mouth and nose
from behind, and struggling to free himself. The police are
satisfied as to the genuineness of his statement.”

“And they have found nothing else?”

“No.”

“Not the Prime Minister’s dead body? Then, there is hope. But it
is strange. Why, after trying to shoot him this morning, are they
now taking so much trouble to keep him alive?”

Dodge shook his head. “One thing’s quite certain. They’re determined
at all costs to prevent his attending the Conference.”

“If it is humanly possible, the Prime Minister shall be there. God
grant it is not too late. Now, messieurs, recount to me
everything—from the beginning. I must know about this shooting
affair as well.”

“Last night, the Prime Minister, accompanied by one of his
secretaries, Captain Daniels——”

“The same who accompanied him to France?”

“Yes. As I was saying, they motored down to Windsor, where the
Prime Minister was granted an Audience. Early this morning, he
returned to town, and it was on the way that the attempted
assassination took place.”

“One moment, if you please. Who is this Captain Daniels? You have
his dossier?”

Lord Estair smiled. “I thought you would ask me that. We do not
know very much of him. He is of no particular family. He has served
in the English Army, and is an extremely able secretary, being an
exceptionally fine linguist. I believe he speaks seven languages.
It is for that reason that the Prime Minister chose him to accompany
him to France.”

“Has he any relatives in England?”

“Two aunts. A Mrs. Everard, who lives at Hampstead, and a Miss
Daniels, who lives near Ascot.”

“Ascot? That is near to Windsor, is it not?”

“That point has not been overlooked. But it has led to nothing.”

“You regard the Capitaine Daniels, then, as above suspicion?”

A shade of bitterness crept into Lord Estair’s voice, as he replied:

“No, Monsieur Poirot. In these days, I should hesitate before I
pronounced _anyone_ above suspicion.”

“_Très bien_. Now I understand, _milord_, that the Prime Minister
would, as a matter of course, be under vigilant police protection,
which ought to render any assault upon him an impossibility?”

Lord Estair bowed his head. “That is so. The Prime Minister’s car
was closely followed by another car containing detectives in plain
clothes. Mr. MacAdam knew nothing of these precautions. He is
personally a most fearless man, and would be inclined to sweep them
away arbitrarily. But, naturally, the police make their own
arrangements. In fact, the Premier’s chauffeur, O’Murphy, is a
C.I.D. man.”

“O’Murphy? That is a name of Ireland, is it not so?”

“Yes, he is an Irishman.”

“From what part of Ireland?”

“County Clare, I believe.”

“_Tiens!_ But proceed, _milord_.”

“The Premier started for London. The car was a closed one. He and
Captain Daniels sat inside. The second car followed as usual. But,
unluckily, for some unknown reason, the Prime Minister’s car
deviated from the main road——”

“At a point where the road curves?” interrupted Poirot.

“Yes—but how did you know?”

“Oh, _c’est évident_! Continue!”

“For some unknown reason,” continued Lord Estair, “the Premier’s
car left the main road. The police car, unaware of the deviation,
continued to keep to the high road. At a short distance down the
unfrequented lane, the Prime Minister’s car was suddenly held up
by a band of masked men. The chauffeur——”

“That brave O’Murphy!” murmured Poirot thoughtfully.

“The chauffeur, momentarily taken aback, jammed on the brakes. The
Prime Minister put his head out of the window. Instantly a shot
rang out—then another. The first one grazed his cheek, the second,
fortunately, went wide. The chauffeur, now realizing the danger,
instantly forged straight ahead, scattering the band of men.”

“A near escape,” I ejaculated, with a shiver.

“Mr. MacAdam refused to make any fuss over the slight wound he had
received. He declared it was only a scratch. He stopped at a local
cottage hospital, where it was dressed and bound up—he did not, of
course, reveal his identity. He then drove, as per schedule,
straight to Charing Cross, where a special train for Dover was
awaiting him, and, after a brief account of what had happened had
been given to the anxious police by Captain Daniels, he duly
departed for France. At Dover, he went on board the waiting
destroyer. At Boulogne, as you know, the bogus car was waiting for
him, carrying the Union Jack, and correct in every detail.”

“That is all you have to tell me?”

“Yes.”

“There is no other circumstance that you have omitted, milord?”

“Well, there is one rather peculiar thing.”

“Yes?”

“The Prime Minister’s car did not return home after leaving the
Prime Minister at Charing Cross. The police were anxious to
interview O’Murphy, so a search was instituted at once. The car
was discovered standing outside a certain unsavoury little
restaurant in Soho, which is well known as a meeting-place of
German agents.”

“And the chauffeur?”

“The chauffeur was nowhere to be found. He, too, had disappeared.”

“So,” said Poirot thoughtfully, “there are two disappearances: the
Prime Minister in France, and O’Murphy in London.”

He looked keenly at Lord Estair, who made a gesture of despair.

“I can only tell you, Monsieur Poirot, that, if anyone had suggested
to me yesterday that O’Murphy was a traitor, I should have laughed
in his face.”

“And to-day?”

“To-day I do not know what to think.”

Poirot nodded gravely. He looked at his turnip of a watch again.

“I understand that I have carte blanche, messieurs—in every way,
I mean? I must be able to go where I choose, and how I choose.”

“Perfectly. There is a special train leaving for Dover in an hour’s
time, with a further contingent from Scotland Yard. You shall be
accompanied by a Military officer and a C.I.D. man, who will hold
themselves at your disposal in every way. Is that satisfactory?”

“Quite. One more question before you leave, messieurs. What made
you come to me? I am unknown, obscure, in this great London of
yours.”

“We sought you out on the express recommendation and wish of a very
great man of your own country.”

“_Comment?_ My old friend the _Préfet_——?”

Lord Estair shook his head.

“One higher than the _Préfet_. One whose word was once law in
Belgium—and shall be again! That England has sworn!”

Poirot’s hand flew swiftly to a dramatic salute. “Amen to that!
Ah, but my Master does not forget. . . . Messieurs, I, Hercule
Poirot, will serve you faithfully. Heaven only send that it will
be in time. But this is dark—dark. . . . I cannot see.”

“Well, Poirot,” I cried impatiently, as the door closed behind the
Ministers, “what do you think?”

My friend was busy packing a minute suitcase, with quick, deft
movements. He shook his head thoughtfully.

“I do not know what to think. My brains desert me.”

“Why, as you said, kidnap him, when a knock on the head would do
as well?” I mused.

“Pardon me, _mon ami_, but I did not quite say that. It is
undoubtedly far more their affair to kidnap him.”

“But why?”

“Because uncertainty creates panic. That is one reason. Were the
Prime Minister dead, it would be a terrible calamity, but the
situation would have to be faced. But now you have paralysis. Will
the Prime Minister reappear, or will he not? Is he dead or alive?
Nobody knows, and until they know nothing definite can be done.
And, as I tell you, uncertainty breeds panic, which is what _les
Boches_ are playing for. Then, again, if the kidnappers are holding
him secretly somewhere, they have the advantage of being able to
make terms with both sides. The German Government is not a liberal
paymaster, as a rule, but no doubt they can be made to disgorge
substantial remittances in such a case as this. Thirdly, they run
no risk of the hangman’s rope. Oh, decidedly, kidnapping is their
affair.”

“Then, if that is so, why should they first try to shoot him?”

Poirot made a gesture of anger. “Ah, that is just what I do not
understand! It is inexplicable—stupid! They have all their
arrangements made (and very good arrangements too!) for the
abduction, and yet they imperil the whole affair by a melodramatic
attack, worthy of a Cinema, and quite as unreal. It is almost
impossible to believe in it, with its band of masked men, not
twenty miles from London!”

“Perhaps they were two quite separate attempts which happened
irrespective of each other,” I suggested.

“Ah, no, that would be too much of a coincidence! Then, further—who
is the traitor? There must have been a traitor—in the first affair,
anyway. But who was it—Daniels or O’Murphy? It must have been one
of the two, or why did the car leave the main road? We cannot
suppose that the Prime Minister connived at his own assassination!
Did O’Murphy take that turning of his own accord, or was it Daniels
who told him to do so?”

“Surely it must have been O’Murphy’s doing.”

“Yes, because if it was Daniels’ the Prime Minister would have
heard the order, and would have asked the reason. But there are
altogether too many ‘whys’ in this affair, and they contradict each
other. If O’Murphy is an honest man, _why_ did he leave the main
road? But if he was a dishonest man, _why_ did he start the car
again when only two shots had been fired—thereby, in all probability,
saving the Prime Minister’s life? And, again, if he was honest,
why did he, immediately on leaving Charing Cross, drive to a
well-known rendezvous of German spies?”

“It looks bad,” I said.

“Let us look at the case with method. What have we for and against
these two men? Take O’Murphy first. Against: that his conduct in
leaving the main road was suspicious; that he is an Irishman from
County Clare; that he has disappeared in a highly suggestive
manner. For: that his promptness in restarting the car saved the
Premier’s life; that he is a Scotland Yard man, and, obviously,
from the post allotted to him, a trusted detective. Now for Daniels.
There is not much against him, except the fact that nothing is
known of his antecedents, and that he speaks too many languages
for a good Englishman! (Pardon me, _mon ami_, but, as linguists,
you are deplorable!) _Now for him_, we have the fact that he was
found gagged, bound, and chloroformed—which does not look as though
he had anything to do with the matter.”

“He might have gagged and bound himself, to divert suspicion.”

Poirot shook his head. “The French police would make no mistake of
that kind. Besides, once he had attained his object, and the Prime
Minister was safely abducted, there would not be much point in his
remaining behind. His accomplices _could_ have gagged and
chloroformed him, of course, but I fail to see what object they
hoped to accomplish by it. He can be of little use to them now,
for, until the circumstances concerning the Prime Minister have
been cleared up, he is bound to be closely watched.”

“Perhaps he hoped to start the police on a false scent?”

“Then why did he not do so? He merely says that something was
pressed over his nose and mouth, and that he remembers nothing
more. There is no false scent there. It sounds remarkably like the
truth.”

“Well,” I said, glancing at the clock, “I suppose we’d better start
for the station. You may find more clues in France.”

“Possibly, _mon ami_, but I doubt it. It is still incredible to me
that the Prime Minister has not been discovered in that limited
area, where the difficulty of concealing him must be tremendous.
If the military and the police of two countries have not found him,
how shall I?”

At Charing Cross we were met by Mr. Dodge.

“This is Detective Barnes, of Scotland Yard, and Major Norman. They
will hold themselves entirely at your disposal. Good luck to you.
It’s a bad business, but I’ve not given up hope. Must be off now.”
And the Minister strode rapidly away.

We chatted in a desultory fashion with Major Norman. In the centre
of the little group of men on the platform I recognized a little
ferret-faced fellow talking to a tall, fair man. He was an old
acquaintance of Poirot’s—Detective-Inspector Japp, supposed to be
one of the smartest of Scotland Yard’s officers. He came over and
greeted my friend cheerfully.

“I heard you were on this job too. Smart bit of work. So far
they’ve got away with the goods all right. But I can’t believe they
can keep him hidden long. Our people are going through France with
a toothcomb. So are the French. I can’t help feeling it’s only a
matter of hours now.”

“That is, if he’s still alive,” remarked the tall detective
gloomily.

Japp’s face fell. “Yes. . . . But somehow I’ve got the feeling he’s
alive all right.”

Poirot nodded. “Yes, yes; he’s alive. But can he be found in time?
I, like you, did not believe he could be hidden so long.”

The whistle blew, and we all trooped up into the Pullman car. Then,
with a slow, unwilling jerk, the train drew out of the station.

It was a curious journey. The Scotland Yard men crowded together.
Maps of Northern France were spread out, and eager forefingers
traced the lines of roads and villages. Each man had his own pet
theory. Poirot showed none of his usual loquacity, but sat staring
in front of him, with an expression on his face that reminded me
of a puzzled child. I talked to Norman, whom I found quite an
amusing fellow. On arriving at Dover Poirot’s behaviour moved me
to intense amusement. The little man, as he went on board the boat,
clutched desperately at my arm. The wind was blowing lustily.

“_Mon Dieu!_” he murmured. “This is terrible!”

“Have courage, Poirot,” I cried. “You will succeed. You will find
him. I am sure of it.”

“Ah, _mon ami_, you mistake my emotion. It is this villainous sea
that troubles me! The _mal de mer_—it is horrible suffering!”

“Oh!” I said, rather taken aback.

The first throb of the engines was felt, and Poirot groaned and
closed his eyes.

“Major Norman has a map of Northern France if you would like to
study it?”

Poirot shook his head impatiently.

“But no, but no! Leave me, my friend. See you, to think, the
stomach and the brain must be in harmony. Laverguier has a method
most excellent for averting the _mal de mer_. You breathe in—and
out—slowly, so—turning the head from left to right and counting
six between each breath.”

I left him to his gymnastic endeavours, and went on deck.

As we came slowly into Boulogne Harbour Poirot appeared, neat and
smiling, and announced to me in a whisper that Laverguier’s system
had succeeded “to a marvel!”

Japp’s forefinger was still tracing imaginary routes on his map.
“Nonsense! The car started from Boulogne—here they branched off.
Now, my idea is that they transferred the Prime Minister to another
car. See?”

“Well,” said the tall detective, “I shall make for the seaports.
Ten to one, they’ve smuggled him on board a ship.”

Japp shook his head. “Too obvious. The order went out at once to
close all the ports.”

The day was just breaking as we landed. Major Norman touched Poirot
on the arm. “There’s a military car here waiting for you, sir.”

“Thank you, monsieur. But, for the moment, I do not propose to
leave Boulogne.”

“What?”

“No, we will enter this hotel here, by the quay.”

He suited the action to the word, demanded and was accorded a
private room. We three followed him, puzzled and uncomprehending.

He shot a quick glance at us. “It is not so that the good detective
should act, eh? I perceive your thought. He must be full of energy.
He must rush to and fro. He should prostrate himself on the dusty
road and seek the marks of tyres through a little glass. He must
gather up the cigarette-end, the fallen match? That is your idea,
is it not?”

His eyes challenged us. “But I—Hercule Poirot—tell you that it is
not so! The true clues are within—_here_!” He tapped his forehead.
“See you, I need not have left London. It would have been sufficient
for me to sit quietly in my rooms there. All that matters is the
little grey cells within. Secretly and silently they do their part,
until suddenly I call for a map, and I lay my finger on a
spot—so—and I say: the Prime Minister is _there_! And it is so!
With method and logic one can accomplish anything! This frantic
rushing to France was a mistake—it is playing a child’s game of
hide-and-seek. But now, though it may be too late, I will set to
work the right way, from within. Silence, my friends, I beg of
you.”

And for five long hours the little man sat motionless, blinking
his eyelids like a cat, his green eyes flickering and becoming
steadily greener and greener. The Scotland Yard man was obviously
contemptuous, Major Norman was bored and impatient, and I myself
found the time pass with wearisome slowness.

Finally, I got up, and strolled as noiselessly as I could to the
window. The matter was becoming a farce. I was secretly concerned
for my friend. If he failed, I would have preferred him to fail in
a less ridiculous manner. Out of the window I idly watched the
daily leave boat, belching forth columns of smoke, as she lay
alongside the quay.

Suddenly I was aroused by Poirot’s voice close to my elbow.

“_Mes amis_, let us start!”

I turned. An extraordinary transformation had come over my friend.
His eyes were flickering with excitement, his chest was swelled to
the uttermost.

“I have been an imbecile, my friends! But I see daylight at last.”

Major Norman moved hastily to the door. “I’ll order the car.”

“There is no need. I shall not use it. Thank Heaven the wind has
fallen.”

“Do you mean you are going to walk, sir?”

“No, my young friend. I am no St. Peter. I prefer to cross the sea
by boat.”

“To cross the _sea_?”

“Yes. To work with method, one must begin from the beginning. And
the beginning of this affair was in England. Therefore, we return
to England.”

At three o’clock, we stood once more upon Charing Cross platform.
To all our expostulations, Poirot turned a deaf ear, and reiterated
again and again that to start at the beginning was not a waste of
time, but the only way. On the way over, he had conferred with
Norman in a low voice, and the latter had despatched a sheaf of
telegrams from Dover.

Owing to the special passes held by Norman, we got through
everywhere in record time. In London, a large police car was
waiting for us, with some plain-clothes men, one of whom handed a
typewritten sheet of paper to my friend. He answered my inquiring
glance.

“A list of the cottage hospitals within a certain radius west of
London. I wired for it from Dover.”

We were whirled rapidly through the London streets. We were on the
Bath Road. On we went, through Hammersmith, Chiswick and Brentford.
I began to see our objective. Through Windsor and on to Ascot. My
heart gave a leap. Ascot was where Daniels had an aunt living. We
were after _him_, then, not O’Murphy.

We duly stopped at the gate of a trim villa. Poirot jumped out and
rang the bell. I saw a perplexed frown dimming the radiance of his
face. Plainly, he was not satisfied. The bell was answered. He was
ushered inside. In a few moments he reappeared, and climbed into
the car with a short, sharp shake of his head. My hopes began to
die down. It was past four now. Even if he found certain evidence
incriminating Daniels, what would be the good of it, unless he
could wring from some one the exact spot in France where they were
holding the Prime Minister?

Our return progress towards London was an interrupted one. We
deviated from the main road more than once, and occasionally
stopped at a small building, which I had no difficulty in
recognizing as a cottage hospital. Poirot only spent a few minutes
at each, but at every halt his radiant assurance was more and more
restored.

He whispered something to Norman, to which the latter replied:

“Yes, if you turn off to the left, you will find them waiting by
the bridge.”

We turned up a side road, and in the failing light I discerned a
second car, waiting by the side of the road. It contained two men
in plain clothes. Poirot got down and spoke to them, and then we
started off in a northerly direction, the other car following close
behind.

We drove for some time, our objective being obviously one of the
northern suburbs of London. Finally, we drove up to the front door
of a tall house, standing a little back from the road in its own
grounds.

Norman and I were left with the car. Poirot and one of the
detectives went up to the door and rang. A neat parlourmaid opened
it. The detective spoke.

“Precisely. Let us go to Hampstead first. I have a small idea.”

“Perhaps. But if so, why did he leave the car in Soho? That seems
to me an unnecessary risk. And then there is the matter of the
second attempt. This is a far more carefully planned affair. The
bogus car, the false A.D.C., the whole thing was admirably done.
What I want to find out is this: did those who kidnapped the Prime
Minister also arrange for the first attempt on his life?”

“You think they did not?”

“I do not know. It is all very confusing. One thing is certain—that
this whole affair is the work of highly intelligent and well-organized
people.”

“Germans?”

“Naturally. But who are the individuals? That is what I have to
discover.”  He snapped his case shut.  “Come, Hastings, we must be
off.”
“Perhaps. But O’Murphy’s disappearance is curious. Why should he
disappear? It is not like a C.I.D. man to disappear. He would be
too valuable to them. And yet, it is highly probable that he _is_
the traitor. But if he is, why should he take the Prime Minister
to a Soho restaurant? That is not the way to dispose of a
Prime Minister. It looks more as if he were meeting someone there
—passing him on to someone else.”

“Then, who is the someone else?” I asked.

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I must find out.”

He closed his bag with a snap.

“Come, Hastings, it is time we departed.”

“Perhaps. But if it was, why did he abandon the car in Soho? It was
a very foolish thing to do, and a most unnecessary risk. One would
have thought that if he were a traitor he would have taken the car
farther away, to some place where it would not be so easily
discovered.”

“But perhaps he was captured and forced to abandon it,” I suggested.


“Possibly. But it is not quite so simple as that.  O’Murphy, being a
policeman, would surely have taken precautions. He would have
informed his superiors.  Why did he not do so?  And, if he were a
traitor, why should he leave the car in such a conspicuous place as
Soho?  It is a very puzzling business, my friend. A very puzzling
business indeed.”  Poirot sighed, and snapped his case shut.  “Come,
let us go.  The train leaves in forty minutes.”
“Yes, because if it was Daniels’ the Prime Minister would have
heard the order, and would have asked the reason. But there are
altogether too many ‘whys’ in this affair, and they contradict each
other. If O’Murphy is an honest man, _why_ did he leave the main
road? But if he was a dishonest man, _why_ did he start the car
again when only two shots had been fired—thereby, in all probability,
saving the Prime Minister’s life? And, again, if he was honest,
why did he, immediately on leaving Charing Cross, drive to a
well-known rendezvous of German spies?”

“It looks bad,” I said.

“Precisely! I propose to go to Boulogne. The bogus A.D.C. and the
bogus car—they interest me exceedingly. The car, you see, was
apparently abandoned. But why abandon a car which has just played
so important a part? There is a lack of method there—a clumsiness.
And then, again, there is the question of the Prime Minister’s
destination. We are told he was going to Versailles. That, also,
requires investigation.”

“You think it possible that he may not have been taken to Versailles
at all?”

“I think it highly probable. Everything points to a carefully laid
plan. But there are several points which are, to say the least,
unaccountable, and it seems to me that someone has blundered. It
is in that blunder, my friend, that I place my hope of finding the
truth.”

“Perhaps. But I have a feeling that the solution of this problem lies
not in France, but in England.  There is something—a detail—which
escapes me.  Something which, if I could only grasp it, would throw
light upon the whole dark business.  This attempted assassination—
it was so clumsy, so amateurish!  And yet the abduction was
masterfully planned and executed.  There is a discrepancy—a
contradiction.  It is that which puzzles me.”  He paused, tapping
his long, elegant fingers on the arm of his chair.  “The whole
affair is wrapped in a fog—but the fog itself is a clue. What is
the nature of the fog?”
“Not yet, my friend. There is still something that puzzles me.
Why should the German agents choose this particular method? Why
kidnap the Prime Minister, when a pistol shot would have served
their purpose equally well? It is all so elaborate, so unnecessarily
complicated. There is something here that I do not understand. It
is too clever, too subtle, for the ordinary German agent.  It is
almost as if they were playing some sort of game—a game of
hide-and-seek with the British police.  And that, my friend, is
what makes me think that perhaps we are looking in the wrong
direction altogether.”
“I shall start for France, certainly, but I shall not neglect
England. There are still some questions that remain to be answered.
Where is O’Murphy? What is the significance of the fact that the
Prime Minister’s car was found outside a German spy rendezvous?
What is the significance of the fact that the abduction took place
in France, and not in England? Why were two attempts made, and why
were they of such a different character? And finally, what part did
Captain Daniels play in the whole affair? These are points which
must be settled before we leave England.”

“But you will not be able to solve them all before we go.”

“I am hopeful, _mon ami_, very hopeful.  We shall see.”  Poirot’s
eyes twinkled.  “Sometimes, a small thing—a seemingly unimportant
detail—is the key to the whole mystery.”

“Exactly! That is precisely what I intend to do.  But first, I must
make a few telephone calls. One to my friend Japp, at Scotland Yard,
and one to Mrs. Everard, Captain Daniels' aunt, at Hampstead.  It
is always wise to begin at the beginning, is it not?”  He picked up
the telephone, his small, neatly-trimmed moustache twitching with
purposeful energy.  “And then,” he added, with a glint in his eye,
“perhaps a small visit to Ascot. One never knows what one might find
buried amongst the heather.”
“Possibly, _mon ami_, but I doubt it. It is still incredible to me
that the Prime Minister has not been discovered in that limited
area, where the difficulty of concealing him must be tremendous.
If the military and the police of two countries have not found him,
how shall I?”

At Charing Cross we were met by Mr. Dodge.

We boarded the train, and settled down in a comfortable carriage.
Poirot, as usual, was meticulously neat and orderly.  He was silent
for a time, seemingly lost in thought.  Then, suddenly, he spoke.
"Hastings," he said, "there is something which puzzles me profoundly
about this affair."

We boarded the train.  Poirot, settling into his corner seat, closed his eyes.  Barnes and Norman, both looking rather grim, exchanged glances.  I, meanwhile, lit a cigarette and watched the English countryside rush past the window, my thoughts swirling around the perplexing details of the case.  The kidnapping, the attempted assassination, the disappearing chauffeur... and the ever-present question: who was the traitor?  Daniels? O'Murphy?  Or was there another player altogether?
We boarded the train, and settled down in a comfortable corner.  Poirot,
despite the gravity of the situation, seemed remarkably calm. He
opened a small, worn leather case and produced a selection of
beautifully-polished manicure implements.  He began meticulously
cleaning his nails.

“You seem remarkably unconcerned, Poirot,” I remarked.

“My dear Hastings,” he replied without looking up, “one must keep
one’s self-respect even in the face of disaster. Besides, the
cleaning of the nails is an occupation of which I am particularly
fond.”

He continued his work with his usual precision.  I watched him,
intrigued by his apparent composure amidst such a crisis.

We boarded the train.  Poirot, surprisingly, seemed less preoccupied
than I expected. He was examining a small, crumpled piece of paper
he had taken from his pocket.  He smoothed it out carefully, and
then, with a magnifying glass, he began to study it minutely.

“What is it, Poirot?” I asked.

He looked up, a gleam in his eye.  “A clue, my friend, perhaps a
very important clue.”

“Where did you get it?”

“From the Minister’s pocket,” he replied with a twinkle.  “When he
was shaking hands he did not observe my dexterity.”
We boarded the train, and, as it sped through the Kent countryside,
Poirot explained his plans.  “First,” he said, “we will go to
Ascot, and visit Miss Daniels. Then, if we are no wiser, we will
visit Mrs. Everard at Hampstead. Then, to Boulogne, to interview
the people who saw the Prime Minister embark on the destroyer.”

“And O’Murphy?” I asked.

“Ah, yes, O’Murphy! I shall deal with him last. He is the most
difficult to understand.  The others, at least, follow a definite
pattern.”

“And Captain Daniels?”

“_Ah, oui!_  He is a curious and interesting case. We shall
investigate his antecedents, if there are any.”


We chatted in a desultory fashion with Major Norman. In the centre
of the little group of men on the platform I recognized a little
ferret-faced fellow talking to a tall, fair man. He was an old
acquaintance of Poirot’s—Detective-Inspector Japp, supposed to be
one of the smartest of Scotland Yard’s officers. He came over and
greeted my friend cheerfully.

Throughout the journey Poirot remained silent and preoccupied.  He
appeared to be wrestling with some difficult problem, and even my
attempts at conversation failed to rouse him from his reverie.  Major
Norman and Detective Barnes, meanwhile, exchanged a few words in
undertones, glancing occasionally at Poirot with an expression of
marked respect.  The atmosphere was one of tense anticipation, broken
only by the rhythmic clatter of the train wheels.
Throughout the journey Poirot remained silent and preoccupied.  He
occasionally consulted a small notebook, making notes with a stubby
pencil.  He scarcely ate anything at lunch, merely sipping a glass
of water.  I tried to engage him in conversation, but he was
unresponsive, his mind clearly far away, grappling with the complexities
of the case.  Major Norman and Detective Barnes, equally silent,
watched him with a mixture of respect and apprehension.  The atmosphere
in the carriage was thick with unspoken anxieties.
During the journey Poirot remained sunk in thought.  He scarcely
spoke, and I forbore to disturb his meditations.  Major Norman
and Detective Barnes were equally silent, their faces betraying
their anxiety.  The atmosphere was heavy with a sense of impending
disaster.  The thought of the approaching Allied Conference, and the
grave consequences of the Prime Minister's absence, hung over us
like a pall.

The journey was uneventful. Poirot spent most of his time looking
out of the window, seemingly lost in thought.  He hardly spoke,
except to ask a few questions of Detective Barnes regarding the
so-called bogus A.D.C. and the abandoned car.  He seemed particularly
interested in the exact location of the farm where Captain Daniels
had been found.  He even requested a map of the area, studying it
with intense concentration.  I, meanwhile, tried to fathom the
mysteries of the case, but the more I thought about it, the more
confused I became.

Throughout the journey Poirot remained sunk in thought. He scarcely
spoke, and when he did, it was only to ask some seemingly trivial
question.  He examined the menu with meticulous care, criticised the
tea, and minutely observed the behaviour of his fellow passengers.  He
even engaged in a brief but intense conversation with the elderly
lady who sat opposite, concerning the merits of various brands of
knitting wool.  To me, his actions seemed strangely out of character,
a deliberate avoidance of the pressing problem at hand.

It was a curious journey. The Scotland Yard men crowded together.
Maps of Northern France were spread out, and eager forefingers
traced the lines of roads and villages. Each man had his own pet
theory. Poirot showed none of his usual loquacity, but sat staring
in front of him, with an expression on his face that reminded me
of a puzzled child. I talked to Norman, whom I found quite an
amusing fellow. On arriving at Dover Poirot’s behaviour moved me
to intense amusement. The little man, as he went on board the boat,
clutched desperately at my arm. The wind was blowing lustily.

“_Mon Dieu!_” he murmured. “This is terrible!”

“Have courage, Poirot,” I cried. “You will succeed. You will find
him. I am sure of it.”

“Ah, _mon ami_, you mistake my emotion. It is this villainous sea
that troubles me! The _mal de mer_—it is horrible suffering!”

“Oh!” I said, rather taken aback.

The first throb of the engines was felt, and Poirot groaned and
closed his eyes.

“Major Norman has a map of Northern France if you would like to
study it?”

Poirot shook his head impatiently.

At Boulogne we were met by a French officer, who conducted us to
General Headquarters. There we found a number of officers and
detectives assembled, and were soon immersed in a mass of
information, or rather misinformation, concerning the case.  The
French authorities, it appeared, were almost as baffled as their
English colleagues.  The only solid fact seemed to be the
discovery of the abandoned car and the chloroformed secretary.  Beyond
that, it was a welter of contradictory statements and unhelpful
leads.
At Boulogne we were met by a French officer, and driven rapidly to
General Headquarters. There we found a number of officers and
detectives assembled, and learnt that the search for the Prime
Minister was still proceeding without success.  Poirot listened
attentively to the reports made, questioning each man shrewdly and
discreetly.  He then made a few brief requests, which were instantly
granted, and left the room.

At Boulogne we were met by a French officer, who, after a brief
consultation with Poirot, bundled us into a waiting car.  The drive
was a fast one, and I gathered that we were headed for the area
where Captain Daniels had been found.  The landscape was bleak and
uninviting, and the countryside, scarred by recent warfare, seemed
to reflect the grimness of our mission.  Poirot, however, remained
uncharacteristically silent, his usual animation replaced by a
preternatural intensity.  His eyes, usually sparkling with
intelligence, now held a steely glint, reflecting the seriousness of
the situation.
At Boulogne we were met by a French officer, who, with a courteous
bow, placed a car at our disposal. We drove to the headquarters
of the French Military authorities, where we were received by a
General. He was a tall, distinguished-looking man, with a charming
manner, and spoke excellent English. After a brief statement of the
case, he said that he had already collected together all the
information that was available. We were then ushered into a room
where a number of officers were assembled. Various maps of the
district covered the walls, and a large-scale plan of a certain
farm lay upon a table.

“This farm,” said the General, pointing to it, “is the place where
Captain Daniels was found. It is an abandoned farm, some miles from
any village or town.”

“And you have searched it thoroughly?” asked Poirot.

“Yes, monsieur. We left no stone unturned. It is absolutely
certain that the Prime Minister is not there.”

At Boulogne we were met by a French officer, who, with a courteous
bow, placed a car at our disposal.  We drove at once to the
General Headquarters, where we were received by General
Berthier.  He was a tall, soldierly-looking man, with a keen,
intelligent face. He greeted Poirot with respect and cordiality.
He expressed his deep concern over the abduction, and his
determination to leave no stone unturned in order to effect the
Prime Minister’s rescue.  He spoke of the search already made with
no result, and of the impossibility of the Prime Minister remaining
undiscovered so long in the confined area.

Japp’s forefinger was still tracing imaginary routes on his map.
“Nonsense! The car started from Boulogne—here they branched off.
Now, my idea is that they transferred the Prime Minister to another
car. See?”

“Well,” said the tall detective, “I shall make for the seaports.
Ten to one, they’ve smuggled him on board a ship.”

Japp shook his head. “Too obvious. The order went out at once to
close all the ports.”

The day was just breaking as we landed. Major Norman touched Poirot
on the arm. “There’s a military car here waiting for you, sir.”

“Thank you, monsieur. But, for the moment, I do not propose to
leave Boulogne.”

“What?”

“No, we will enter this hotel here, by the quay.”

He suited the action to the word, demanded and was accorded a
private room. We three followed him, puzzled and uncomprehending.

Japp grinned.  "Something like that, Monsieur Poirot.  Though I must admit, I'd rather be doing it than sitting here."  He looked around the comfortably furnished room with a sigh.

Poirot smiled serenely.  "Patience, my friend.  Patience.  We have first to consider the facts.  We have a missing Prime Minister, a missing chauffeur, and a missing car.  We also have a Captain Daniels, conveniently chloroformed, and a number of unanswered questions."
Japp grinned.  "Something like that, Monsieur Poirot.  Though I must admit, I haven't had time for the cigarette ends yet."  He chuckled.  "But you're not going to sit here and do nothing, are you?"
Japp grinned. “Something like that, sir.”

“_Mais non!_” cried Poirot, waving a hand. “We will sit quietly
here and think. We will reflect. We will use our brains. We will
consider what the others have not considered. Now, my friends,
tell me—what is the first thing you did on arriving at Boulogne?”

“I went to General Headquarters,” said Major Norman.

“And you?” asked Poirot, turning to Japp.

“Same as the Major. Went to G.H.Q.”

Poirot smiled, a slow, enigmatic smile.  “And what did they tell
you at G.H.Q.?”

We murmured our assent. Poirot smiled.  “_Mais non!_  That is not
my method. I prefer to sit quietly and think. I have a little
suspicion. . . a little idea. . . .  It is necessary that I
should reflect. I require a comfortable chair, a cup of coffee,
and—above all—silence!”

He settled himself comfortably in the armchair, closed his eyes, and
remained silent for a long time.  Major Norman and Detective Barnes
exchanged glances.  I lit a cigarette and watched the little man
intently.

Japp grinned.  "Something like that, yes."

Poirot chuckled.  "But no, my friends.  The great detective is
sometimes a very lazy man. He sits and thinks. He observes. He waits.
And now, messieurs, I propose to wait." He settled himself comfortably
in an armchair, his eyes fixed on the bustling activity of the quayside.

His eyes challenged us. “But I—Hercule Poirot—tell you that it is
not so! The true clues are within—_here_!” He tapped his forehead.
“See you, I need not have left London. It would have been sufficient
for me to sit quietly in my rooms there. All that matters is the
little grey cells within. Secretly and silently they do their part,
until suddenly I call for a map, and I lay my finger on a
spot—so—and I say: the Prime Minister is _there_! And it is so!
With method and logic one can accomplish anything! This frantic
rushing to France was a mistake—it is playing a child’s game of
hide-and-seek. But now, though it may be too late, I will set to
work the right way, from within. Silence, my friends, I beg of
you.”

Suddenly, Poirot sprang to his feet.  "The telegram!" he exclaimed,
snapping his fingers. "The telegram from the abandoned farm near C——!
It mentioned nothing of the car, only the chloroformed secretary.
Why? Because the car was not there!  It was a blind!"

Suddenly, Poirot sprang to his feet.  He picked up the telephone and
spoke rapidly in French. Then, he hung up, and, with a triumphant
smile, turned to us. "It is settled.  We leave at once for
Amiens."
Suddenly, Poirot sprang to his feet.  He snatched up a pen and a
piece of paper, and began to write rapidly.  He scribbled down a
series of names and addresses, pausing occasionally to make a
vigorous notation.  When he had finished, he looked up, a triumphant
gleam in his eye.

"That is it, mes amis," he declared. "We start at once."

Suddenly Poirot sat bolt upright.  He snapped his fingers.  "Voilà!" he
exclaimed, his voice vibrant with excitement.  "I have it! The
solution is clear as crystal!" He began to pace the room, his
characteristic little moustache bristling with energy.

Suddenly Poirot sprang to his feet.  He snatched up a newspaper
that lay on the table, his eyes gleaming with triumph.  He pointed a
trembling finger at a small paragraph tucked away in a corner.  "There!" he exclaimed, his voice barely above a whisper. "There is the answer!"
Finally, I got up, and strolled as noiselessly as I could to the
window. The matter was becoming a farce. I was secretly concerned
for my friend. If he failed, I would have preferred him to fail in
a less ridiculous manner. Out of the window I idly watched the
daily leave boat, belching forth columns of smoke, as she lay
alongside the quay.

Suddenly I was aroused by Poirot’s voice close to my elbow.

“_Mes amis_, let us start!”

I turned. An extraordinary transformation had come over my friend.
His eyes were flickering with excitement, his chest was swelled to
the uttermost.

“I have been an imbecile, my friends! But I see daylight at last.”

Major Norman moved hastily to the door. “I’ll order the car.”

“There is no need. I shall not use it. Thank Heaven the wind has
fallen.”

“Do you mean you are going to walk, sir?”

“No, my young friend. I am no St. Peter. I prefer to cross the sea
by boat.”

“To cross the _sea_?”

“Yes. To work with method, one must begin from the beginning. And
the beginning of this affair was in England. Therefore, we return
to England.”

“Now, mes amis,” said Poirot, “we go to Hampstead. To Mrs. Everard’s
house.”  He spoke with an air of quiet confidence that was
completely at variance with his previous state of bewilderment.  The
change was so sudden and so complete that it was almost uncanny.
  
“First,” said Poirot, “we shall visit Captain Daniels’ aunt, Mrs.
Everard. Hampstead, was it not?”  He consulted a small,
leather-bound notebook.  “Number 17, Holly Bush Lane.  A most
convenient address.”  He consulted his watch.  “It is now 3:45.  We
shall arrive in good time for tea.”
“Now, my friends,” said Poirot, briskly, “we proceed to Hampstead.
To Mrs. Everard’s.”  He spoke with a sudden decisiveness that
startled me.  Until now, his actions had seemed almost whimsical,
a curious counterpoint to the gravity of the situation.  This
sharp change of tone suggested a sudden clarity of thought, a
concrete plan finally forming in his mind.
“Now, mes amis,” said Poirot briskly, “we proceed to Hampstead.
To Mrs. Everard’s.”  He spoke with such quiet confidence that even
the sceptical Detective Barnes seemed impressed.  The car was
waiting, and we set off without further discussion.

“Now, my friends,” said Poirot, “we go to Hampstead. To Mrs.
Everard’s.”  The Scotland Yard man looked surprised. “But surely,
sir, we should be getting on with the Boulogne inquiries. We’ve lost
a whole day already.”  Poirot smiled enigmatically. “We waste no
time, my friend. We shall be in Boulogne to-morrow—perhaps.”  He

Owing to the special passes held by Norman, we got through
everywhere in record time. In London, a large police car was
waiting for us, with some plain-clothes men, one of whom handed a
typewritten sheet of paper to my friend. He answered my inquiring
glance.

“A list of the cottage hospitals within a certain radius west of
London. I wired for it from Dover.”

The car stopped outside a small, rather dilapidated cottage. Poirot
jumped out, and beckoned us to follow. He was leading us to the
house of Miss Daniels, the aunt of Captain Daniels. He rang the bell
with a firm hand. A rather nervous-looking woman opened the door.
Poirot produced his credentials.  The woman looked flustered and
agitated.

We stopped outside a small cottage hospital, almost hidden amongst
the trees. Poirot sprang out. “_Voilà!_” he cried triumphantly.
“This is it. Now, you two remain here and await my return. I shall
not be long.”  He disappeared inside, leaving us to stare after
him in utter bewilderment.


We stopped outside a small cottage hospital. Poirot, with a swift,
decisive movement, leaped out. He was inside the building before I
had time to follow him. In a few seconds he was back again, his face
radiant.

“_Voilà!_” he cried. “It is solved!”

“What do you mean?”

“I shall tell you presently. Get into the car, and we will drive
to Hampstead. Quick!”

The car stopped outside a small cottage hospital, and Poirot, with
an air of quiet determination, entered. He was gone for about half
an hour. Then he emerged, followed by a very scared nurse and a
very surprised-looking doctor.  He spoke a few words to them, and
then turned to us with a smile.  "The game is up," he announced.

At a certain point on the road, Poirot ordered the car to stop.
He pointed to a small, almost insignificant lane branching off to
the right, overgrown with weeds and bordered by tall hedges.

“This is the lane,” he said. “This is where the Prime Minister’s
car left the main road. Notice the tracks in the soft earth.”

We duly stopped at the gate of a trim villa. Poirot jumped out and
rang the bell. I saw a perplexed frown dimming the radiance of his
face. Plainly, he was not satisfied. The bell was answered. He was
ushered inside. In a few moments he reappeared, and climbed into
the car with a short, sharp shake of his head. My hopes began to
die down. It was past four now. Even if he found certain evidence
incriminating Daniels, what would be the good of it, unless he
could wring from some one the exact spot in France where they were
holding the Prime Minister?

We reached the bridge. A motor-car was waiting there. In it were
seated two men—Lord Estair and Mr. Dodge. Their faces were drawn
and anxious.  Lord Estair leaned forward.

“Monsieur Poirot, we have just received a message from France. The
Prime Minister has been found!”

“_Ah!_” cried Poirot triumphantly, his eyes sparkling like a child’s.
“And where, _milord_?”

“At a small chateau near Fontainebleau. He is perfectly safe. They
had him hidden in the cellars.”

“But how?”

“A young woman, a German agent, was apprehended last night. She
confessed.”

At length we arrived at a small village, and, leaving the car, we
proceeded on foot down a lane. As we walked, Poirot hummed
tunelessly to himself, a low, satisfied rumble in his throat. At
the end of the lane was a bridge. On the other side of the bridge
stood two figures, a tall man and a woman. The tall man was Japp,
and the woman was Mrs. Everard, Captain Daniels’ aunt.

We arrived at a small bridge spanning a narrow stream. A car was
waiting there, and in it sat two men—Japp and a woman. The woman
was stout and elderly. She wore a severe black dress, and her face
was concealed behind a thick veil. Japp, his face aglow with
triumph, jumped out.

“We’ve got her, Poirot,” he exclaimed. “The old girl’s the real
article.”

“Frau Bertha Ebenthal?”

“The same. And, what’s more, we’ve got the goods, too.”

“_Magnifique!_” cried Poirot.

We turned off at a crossroads, and presently drew up outside a small,
picturesque inn. A tall, fair man stepped out to meet us. It was
Japp. His usually cheerful face was drawn and anxious.

“We’ve got him, sir,” he said, speaking to Poirot. “But we haven’t
got the Prime Minister. He’s vanished again!”

“Vanished?” exclaimed Poirot. “But how?”

“We found him here—in a room upstairs. The man who had him—a
German agent, naturally—Frau Bertha Ebenthal, had apparently left
him there while she went to get some food. The police raided the
place about an hour ago. But he’s gone! The window was open, and he
was gone. No trace of him—except for the fellow we’ve got.”

We drove on in silence for a few minutes. Then Poirot suddenly
leaned forward and tapped the chauffeur on the shoulder.

“Stop here, my friend. We alight.”

He stepped out, and I followed him. We were by the side of a small
stream, which had been swollen by recent rains. The water was
running rapidly, carrying down with it various twigs and pieces of
rubbish.

“_Voilà!_” cried Poirot triumphantly.

He pointed to a small, muddy object which was being carried along
by the current.

“A button!” I exclaimed. “A rather unusual button. It appears to be
covered with some kind of fur. A very curious kind of button. A sort
of dark grey fur, with white spots on it.”

“_Précisément!_”

“What do you make of it?”

“_Mon ami_, I make of it that it is from the coat of a German
officer—a Uhlan! But the button itself is unique. It is, as you
see, of English make. I could almost wager it was made for a
uniform. _Tiens!_ It carries me back to other days, and to a
particular woman. _Oui_, a particular woman! Frau Bertha Ebenthal.
She once came to me at the request of my old friend the _Préfet_.
She was a very remarkable woman, _cette_ Frau Ebenthal! I have not
forgotten her.”

We turned up a side road, and in the failing light I discerned a
second car, waiting by the side of the road. It contained two men
in plain clothes. Poirot got down and spoke to them, and then we
started off in a northerly direction, the other car following close
behind.

We waited for some time.  Then Poirot emerged, his face alight with
triumph, followed by the tall woman and the two detectives who had
gone in with him. The woman was handcuffed.  I recognized her at
once. She was Frau Bertha Ebenthal, the notorious German spy.

We waited for what seemed an interminable time. Then the door opened
and Poirot appeared, followed by the tall woman and the parlourmaid.
The woman was in a state of great agitation, but she carried
herself with a certain dignity. The parlourmaid was completely
hysterical.

“This is Frau Bertha Ebenthal,” said Poirot, indicating the woman.
“And the house, as you may guess, is hers.”

We waited patiently in the car. It seemed an eternity. Then, at
last, the door opened, and Poirot came out, followed by the tall,
handsome woman, who was being supported by one of the detectives.
She was weeping silently.  Poirot smiled triumphantly.

“_Voilà!_” he exclaimed, as he got into the car. “The bird is
caught!”

“Frau Bertha Ebenthal?” I queried, recognizing the name from
somewhere.

“The same.  A highly skilled chemist, _mon ami_. A most valuable
asset to the enemy during the war, I assure you.”

“But how. . . ?”

“_Patience_, my friend. All will be revealed in due course.”

In a few moments Poirot reappeared, and beckoned us to follow him.
We entered the house. The tall woman was sitting in a chair, her
face ashen, her eyes fixed upon Poirot with a look of intense
hatred. In the room were several men in plain clothes. The air was
thick with the smell of chloroform.  On a large sofa lay a man,
apparently unconscious.  He was bound and gagged.

We waited for what seemed an interminable time. Then the door opened
again, and Poirot emerged, followed by the tall woman, who was
evidently Frau Bertha Ebenthal, and the parlourmaid, who was
carrying a small, black hand-bag.  Poirot beckoned us forward.

“_Voilà!_” he announced triumphantly, holding up the hand-bag.
“The missing person has been found, _mes amis_!”

I could not speak. I was too utterly surprised.

“But where?” I gasped, at last.

“In here,” he answered, tapping the hand-bag. “In this little hand-bag,
so cunningly contrived. The woman is a clever one. But she did not
outwit _me_.”

Norman and I spent about five minutes cursing our forced inactivity.
Finally the door reopened, and the men emerged, escorting three
prisoners—a woman and two men. The woman, and one of the men, were
taken to the second car. The other man was placed in our car by
Poirot himself.

“I must go with the others, my friend. But have great care of this
gentleman. You do not know him, no? _Eh bien_, let me present to
you, Monsieur O’Murphy!”

We drove to Scotland Yard. There, in a private room, Poirot
explained everything.  The woman was Frau Bertha Ebenthal, a notorious
German agent. The other man was her secretary.  O’Murphy, it
transpired, had been completely innocent of any wrongdoing.

We drove back to Scotland Yard. There, in a private room, Poirot
explained everything.  The woman was Frau Bertha Ebenthal, a
notorious German spy, and her companion was Captain Daniels, her
willing accomplice.  The seemingly random attacks, the misleading
clues, the elaborate kidnapping – it was all a carefully orchestrated
distraction.

We drove back to Scotland Yard.  Poirot, having left us at the
corner, went on alone.  I felt a growing excitement. The mystery
was nearly solved.  The capture of O’Murphy, the visit to the
hospitals, the trip to Ascot – it all pointed to a carefully
constructed plan, a plan that was now, I felt, about to unravel.

“Now, Hastings,” said Poirot, leaning back in his seat, “let us
discuss the matter. You perceive, my friend, that the kidnapping
of the Prime Minister was a very clever affair, very well planned,
and, but for one little oversight, would have been a complete
success.  But there was this one little oversight.”

He paused, and then added with a triumphant smile:  “The
oversight of Frau Bertha Ebenthal.”

We drove to Scotland Yard.  The atmosphere there was one of
intense excitement.  Poirot was immediately ushered into a private
room, while Norman and I were left to wait.  After what seemed an
eternity, he emerged, looking utterly exhausted but triumphant.  He
summoned us, and we followed him to another room, where a small
group of men were assembled.

To my surprise, we still kept a northerly route. We were not
returning to London, then! I was much puzzled. Suddenly, as the
car slowed down, I recognized that we were close to Hendon
Aerodrome. Immediately I grasped Poirot’s idea. He proposed to
reach France by aeroplane.

It was a sporting idea, but, on the face of it, impracticable. A
telegram would be far quicker. Time was everything. He must leave
the personal glory of rescuing the Prime Minister to others.

As we drew up, Major Norman jumped out, and a plain-clothes man
took his place. He conferred with Poirot for a few minutes, and
then went off briskly.

I, too, jumped out, and caught Poirot by the arm.

“I congratulate you, old fellow! They have told you the hiding-place?
But, look here, you must wire to France at once. You’ll be too late
if you go yourself.”

Poirot looked at me curiously for a minute or two.

“Unfortunately, my friend, there are some things that cannot be
sent by telegram.”

At that moment Major Norman returned, accompanied by a young
officer in the uniform of the Flying Corps.

“This is Captain Lyall, who will fly you over to France. He can
start at once.”

“Wrap up warmly, sir,” said the young pilot. “I can lend you a
coat, if you like.”

He indicated O’Murphy, who sat like a graven image, seemingly
unaware of what was happening. O’Murphy looked up, startled.  He
protested with a muttered oath, but Poirot silenced him with a
gesture.  "It is useless, my friend.  You have but one course open
to you now.  To cooperate."

He indicated O’Murphy, who had not moved or spoken throughout.  The
Irishman looked up, startled.  A flicker of something—fear?—crossed
his face.  He opened his mouth to speak, but Poirot silenced him
with a raised hand.  "It is essential, monsieur, that you should
reach the scene of the crime without delay."

He indicated O’Murphy, who had not moved or spoken throughout the
whole proceedings. O’Murphy looked up in astonishment. Then he
burst into a torrent of expletives. I could not hear much of what
he said, but it was plain that he was not pleased at being bundled
into an aeroplane. However, there was nothing for it but to
obey.  He was hustled into the machine.  The engine roared, and
then, with a final wave from Poirot, the aeroplane soared into
the air.

He indicated O’Murphy, who was still sitting like a lump in the car.
O’Murphy stared at him with an expression of blank amazement, and
then, with a sudden burst of energy, sprang to his feet.

“What’s this? What’s the game?”

“_Silence, monsieur_,” said Poirot. “You will be more comfortable
in the aeroplane than here.”

He indicated O’Murphy, who had remained perfectly passive during
this colloquy. The Irishman looked up, startled.  He opened his
mouth to speak, but Poirot silenced him with a raised hand.

“It is imperative, monsieur, that you proceed to France without
delay.  Your presence there is urgently required.”

He moved a little aside as he spoke, and a figure came forward out
of the darkness. It was the second male prisoner who had gone in
the other car, and as the light fell on his face, I gave a gasp of
surprise.

_It was the Prime Minister!_

“For Heaven’s sake, tell me all about it,” I cried impatiently, as
Poirot, Norman, and I motored back to London. “How in the world
did they manage to smuggle him back to England?”

“There was no need to smuggle him back,” replied Poirot dryly. “The
Prime Minister has never left England. He was kidnapped on his way
from Windsor to London.”

“What?”

“I will make all clear. The Prime Minister was in his car, his
secretary beside him. Suddenly a pad of chloroform is clapped on
his face——”

“But by whom?”

“Not at all. The substitutes were Frau Bertha Ebenthal, a German
spy, disguised as the Prime Minister, and a certain Herr
Schmidt—a remarkably clever mimic—disguised as Captain Daniels.
The real Daniels was chloroformed, bound, and gagged, and left by
the roadside, to be found later by the police. The bogus Prime
Minister and the bogus Daniels arrived at Charing Cross, took the
train to Dover, and embarked upon the destroyer. The bogus A.D.C.
and the bogus car were waiting for them at Boulogne.”

“But what about O’Murphy?”

“O’Murphy was in the plot all along. He was in the pay of the
Germans, and knew his way about. It was an easy thing for him to
drive the car to a rendezvous, abandon the car, and disappear.”

“And the attempt on the Prime Minister’s life?”

“That was the work of a separate gang—a preliminary attempt, which
failed. It had nothing to do with the kidnapping. It was only
meant to provide a diversion. You see, it was the work of those who
wanted the Prime Minister dead, not those who wanted him kept alive
as a hostage.”

“But how did you find out?”

“I asked the obvious question, my friend.”

“What was that?”

“Where is he?”


  •   •   •   •   •   •   •

“_Mais non!_ It is quite simple. The substitutes were Frau Bertha
Ebenthal, a German spy, disguised as the Prime Minister, and a
young man, also a German agent, disguised as Captain Daniels. The
real Daniels, meanwhile, was bound and gagged, and chloroformed, by
O’Murphy, in the side road. The plan was perfectly conceived. It was
a bold stroke, and, had it not been for one flaw, it would have
succeeded.”

“What flaw?”

“The flaw was O’Murphy’s appearance at the German rendezvous in
Soho. He went there to inform his employers that the job was
accomplished, and to receive his instructions. This was his fatal
mistake. For it was that which led to his discovery and arrest.”

“But why did he do it?”

“Because he was a traitor. He was not a loyal Scotland Yard man. He
was a traitor from County Clare, a man who has long been in the pay
of Germany.”

“And Frau Ebenthal?”

“She was to represent the Prime Minister at the Conference, and
to make a speech—a speech calculated to produce a premature and
disastrous peace.”

“But what about Captain Daniels?”

“Not at all. The substitutes were Frau Bertha Ebenthal, a German
spy, disguised as the Prime Minister, and a certain Mr. Schmidt,
disguised as Captain Daniels. The real Captain Daniels was already
a prisoner, gagged and bound, in the second car. The German agents
had had sufficient time to secure his person, having had access to
him at Ascot, where he was staying with an aunt, and having
apparently gained his confidence by a forged letter, which purported
to be from his other aunt—Mrs. Everard—in London. The substitute
Daniels, with the bogus Prime Minister, crossed to France. The
real Prime Minister, meanwhile, was driven to a house in the north
of London, and kept a prisoner there until Poirot got on the trail.
He had a certain clue which he did not wish to explain. It concerned
the cottage hospitals. It had revealed the fact that the Prime
Minister had his wound dressed at a cottage hospital. This showed
that he could not have been kidnapped in France.”

“But O’Murphy?”

“Ah, yes. O’Murphy is an Irishman, and the German agents had
bought him. He was allowed to leave the scene of the crime, so as
to divert suspicion from himself.”

“Then the attempt to shoot the Prime Minister was a mere accident,
a blunder?”

“Precisely. The German agents had made all their plans for the
kidnapping. The shooting was an independent incident. It was pure
luck that the Prime Minister was not killed.”

“And Frau Ebenthal?”

“Frau Ebenthal, having satisfactorily played her part, was then
taken back to England, to be deported.”

“And the German agents?”

“Their plans were foiled. The Conference was saved.”

“But how did you discover all this?”

“Ah, _mon ami_, that is a long story. It began when I was given
the dossier on Captain Daniels. From there it went to the cottage
hospitals, to O’Murphy, and then to the lady in Hampstead. All
very simple, when you know how.”

“Not at all. The substitutes were Frau Bertha Ebenthal, a German
spy, disguised as the Prime Minister, and a certain individual
posing as Captain Daniels. The real Daniels was chloroformed and
hidden. The bogus Prime Minister and bogus Daniels were taken to
Frau Ebenthal’s house.  The real Prime Minister and O’Murphy,
meanwhile, were hidden in a small cottage hospital, where a slight
wound received by the Prime Minister was dressed.”

“But why the attempted assassination?”

“That was a blind.  To throw the police off the scent.”

“Not at all. The substitutes were Frau Bertha Ebenthal, a German
agent, disguised as the Prime Minister, and a certain Mr.
Schneider, disguised as Captain Daniels. The real Daniels, of
course, was chloroformed, gagged, and bound by his accomplices
before they started their journey.  The whole thing was incredibly
well-planned. The shooting affair was a blind. The bogus car and
A.D.C. were also part of the plan to cover their tracks.  It was
Frau Ebenthal who fired the shots. She's a crack shot.”

“_Pas du tout!_ Have you not seen music-hall turns imitating
celebrities with marvellous accuracy? Nothing is easier than to
personate a public character. The Prime Minister of England is far
easier to understudy than Mr. John Smith of Clapham, say. As for
O’Murphy’s ‘double,’ no one was going to take much notice of him
until after the departure of the Prime Minister, and by then he
would have made himself scarce. He drives straight from Charing
Cross to the meeting-place of his friends. He goes in as O’Murphy,
he emerges as some one quite different. O’Murphy has disappeared,
leaving a conveniently suspicious trail behind him.”

“But the man who personated the Prime Minister was seen by every
one!”

“Is a certain Herr Doktor Josef, a German agent, who is an
extraordinary mimic. He is now safely in custody. The woman in the
house is Frau Bertha Ebenthal, his accomplice.  She is a distant
relative of Captain Daniels' other aunt, Mrs. Everard.  She provided
the safe house and assisted in the deception.  The entire operation
was planned and executed by these three, in collaboration with
O’Murphy, who was, as you suspected, a traitor.”

“Is a certain Herr Doktor Josef, a German agent who has been in
England for some time, and who bears a most extraordinary likeness
to Mr. MacAdam.  He is a man of considerable intelligence and
resource. The two women, Frau Bertha Ebenthal and Mrs. Everard, are
his accomplices.  Frau Ebenthal is his wife, and Mrs. Everard is
Captain Daniels’ aunt.  She provided the necessary introductions
and a safe house.”

“Is a certain Herr Schultz, a German agent, who has been living
in England for years. He is an extraordinarily clever mimic, and
has been carefully coached for his part by Frau Bertha Ebenthal, a
woman who is a noted teacher of elocution and dramatic art. He was
taken to a cottage hospital near Windsor for treatment after the
first assault, and his wound was dressed by a doctor who is also in
the conspiracy. The same doctor attended to the false Prime
Minister at Boulogne.”

“But what was the object of all this elaborate deception?”

“Is a German agent, Frau Bertha Ebenthal, disguised as a man. A
remarkably clever woman, I assure you. She has been in England for
many years. She has a small villa at Hampstead, where she lives
with her niece and another woman—the other prisoner. The niece
is Mrs. Everard, an aunt of Captain Daniels. They were all in it
together—a well-organized gang. They planned to keep the Prime
Minister a prisoner until after the Conference was over. Then
they proposed to make certain demands upon the British Government.
Their intentions were, of course, to make a good deal of money. But
moreover, to cause a great deal of trouble in the country.”

“But why did they attempt to shoot him?”

“That was not part of the original scheme. It was the work of
another and independent gang of German agents. It is to be hoped
that they will be caught as well.”

“And O’Murphy?”

“He knew nothing whatever about it. He was a perfectly honest
officer. Frau Ebenthal managed to get hold of him and keep him
quiet by threats.”

“Is Frau Bertha Ebenthal, a German spy of long standing, and
remarkably like the Prime Minister in appearance. She is a clever
woman and a daring one, but she is not a good actress. She overacted
her part in a subtle manner. That is what betrayed her.”

“How did you find her out?”

“I studied all the cottage hospitals within a certain radius of
London. At one of them, the Prime Minister had undergone a slight
operation for the removal of a small growth on his throat. Frau
Ebenthal had no such growth.”

“Then how did you discover she was in England?”

“Rids himself of his disguise. He and the bogus chauffeur may be
arrested as suspicious characters, but no one will dream of
suspecting their real part in the drama, and they will eventually
be released for lack of evidence.”

“And the real Prime Minister?”

“When I heard that the Prime Minister’s car had been found outside
a notorious rendezvous of German agents. It was then that I began
to suspect O’Murphy. But when I heard that the Prime Minister’s
secretary, Captain Daniels, spoke seven languages, I knew that the
key to the mystery lay in him. That, and the fact that he had an
aunt at Ascot, near Windsor, and that the attack had taken place
near there.  It was too convenient. The cottage hospitals were a
red herring, of course—a blind to throw the police off the track.
The real clue was the fact that the Prime Minister had attended an
audience at Windsor the previous evening, and therefore was not
expected back in London at the time of the so-called assassination
attempt. The whole thing was a beautifully planned scheme.”

“When I saw that the assassination attempt was so clumsily
managed. It was too obvious. It was a blind. Then, again, the
Prime Minister’s car did not return to Downing Street after leaving
him at Charing Cross. That was suspicious. And, finally, the
telegram from France describing Daniels’ condition.  It was too
pat. Too carefully planned. It had the hallmarks of a deliberate
misdirection. That is why I insisted on returning to England.  I
knew, instinctively, that the solution lay there.”

“When I considered the attempted assassination. It was too
melodramatic, too theatrical. It was not the work of experienced
agents. Then, I considered O’Murphy’s disappearance. It was
too—obvious. I realized that they were trying to create a
diversion—that O’Murphy was innocent. The real traitor was
Daniels, and the whole thing was a cleverly planned scheme to
prevent the Prime Minister from attending the conference. The
cottage hospitals gave me the clue. The Prime Minister’s slight
wound was treated at one of them. The rest was deduction.”

“When I noticed the discrepancy in the times. The attempted
assassination took place at approximately 8:15 a.m. The Prime
Minister reached Charing Cross at 9:00 a.m. He must have been
kidnapped _before_ 8:15 a.m., for he must have been unconscious
before the attack. It was a prearranged thing. And, as I say, there
were too many whys. In fact, the whole thing was not a kidnapping,
but a carefully rehearsed impersonation. I knew that the Prime
Minister must be somewhere near London. The only logical place to
keep him hidden safely was in a house where a friendly woman was
waiting to look after him. The woman was to be trusted. Who could
I turn to but the one who is in the conspiracy herself?  The
suspicious aunt.”

“When I saw the telegram from France announcing the discovery of
Daniels, gagged and bound. It was too neat. It was too well done.
It was the work of an amateur. An expert would have left the
details of the plot more obscure. Then, again, the fact that the
Prime Minister had been to Windsor and was returning to London that
morning—why should he be going in that direction at that hour?
Only one person could know of that appointment—the traitor himself.
He was not O’Murphy—O’Murphy was too brave. It must be Daniels,
and the point of his aunt’s presence at Hampstead immediately
occurred to me.”

“But how did you find out about Frau Ebenthal?”

“When I began to work the right way—from _within_! I could not make
that shooting affair fit in—but when I saw that the net result of
it was that _the Prime Minister went to France with his face bound
up_ I began to comprehend! And when I visited all the cottage
hospitals between Windsor and London, and found that no one
answering to my description had had his face bound up and dressed
that morning, I was sure! After that, it was child’s-play for a
mind like mine!”

The following morning, Poirot showed me a telegram he had just
received. It had no place of origin, and was unsigned. It ran:

“In time.”
